name: Design, Plan-Check, and Construction Timelines for ADUs
headline: Design, Plan-Check, and Construction Timelines for ADUs
articleBody: ### Typical Timelines for ADU Design and Permitting California’s ADU statutes impose deadline requirements on local agencies: once a **complete ADU application** is submitted, the city or county must approve or deny the project within a fixed number of days using a ministerial process, provided the proposal meets objective standards. State HCD guidance notes that jurisdictions generally have 60 days to act on a complete ADU application, though processing can be paused if the submittal is deemed incomplete and corrections are requested. In practice, Los Angeles-area planning and building departments publish internal targets and report variable turnaround times depending on workload. Local ADU builders and design firms commonly describe a **design and plan development period** of roughly 4–12 weeks for site measurements, conceptual layouts, code review, construction documents, and engineering, depending on project complexity and the number of homeowner revisions. Pre-approved standard plans offered by Los Angeles County can shorten the design phase by reducing architectural drafting, though site-specific plotting and coordination still require several weeks in many cases. Plan-check cycles add more time. Public Works and city building safety divisions often complete first plan review within a few weeks, followed by correction cycles. Industry experience shared by ADU-dedicated firms in Los Angeles suggests total permitting durations of approximately 2–4 months for straightforward projects, and longer for hillside sites, historic properties, or lots with complex setbacks and easements. Construction itself typically ranges from 4–9 months depending on whether the ADU is a garage conversion, ground-up detached unit, or two-story addition. An ADU design contractor’s role includes front-loading code compliance in the drawings to reduce correction rounds, coordinating timely responses to plan-check comments, and setting realistic expectations that the statutory decision deadline applies only after the submittal is deemed complete by the jurisdiction.
